name: Evergreen Protocol Definitions
description: Canonical definitions index for Evergreen Protocol v1.0 — the category standard for reference continuity governance.
usageNotice: Static versioned reference. Not a certification, compliance verdict, or live API endpoint.

terms.definition: The governance discipline of maintaining the validity, version integrity, citeability, and operational coherence of institutional reference systems — protocols, knowledge bases, evidence layers, and documentation — under accelerated change.
terms.boundaryNote: Reference continuity is the category Evergreen Protocol governs. It does not encompass information security, data governance, AI model safety, or content management.

terms.definition: The gradual loss of validity, citeability, or operational coherence in a reference system. Occurs silently through outdated content, undocumented changes, ambiguous ownership, or disconnection from the practices it governs. The primary risk that reference continuity governance addresses.
terms.boundaryNote: Reference decay describes a governance risk in reference systems only. It is not a security incident, legal finding, or compliance verdict.

terms.definition: The challenge of maintaining reference validity in institutional environments where AI models, outputs, tools, team configurations, and regulatory frameworks change faster than the governance structures that depend on them. AI-era conditions accelerate reference decay; they do not constitute a separate governance category.
terms.boundaryNote: AI-era digital continuity frames accelerated reference change. It does not evaluate AI models, certify AI systems, or define AI safety controls.

terms.definition: A versioned, citable reference that defines the scope, vocabulary, and explicit boundaries of a specific governance category. A category standard does not certify, audit, or impose legal obligations; it defines and documents a category.
terms.boundaryNote: A category standard defines and documents a category. It does not certify, audit, impose legal obligations, or open a compliance registry.

terms.definition: A documented unit of governance with bounded scope, named roles, listed artifacts, acceptance criteria, and a defined review and versioning regime. A pattern for maintaining validity across time — not a claim about any specific technology or product category.
terms.boundaryNote: This term describes a governance pattern within the standard. It is not a product category, certification mark, or external recognition claim.

terms.definition: The structural layer: the formal elements — charter, roles, artifacts, acceptance criteria, change control — that give continuity a stable shape. Defines what may be built and audited.
terms.boundaryNote: This layer structures reference governance only. It does not prescribe software architecture, security architecture, or implementation tooling.

terms.definition: The philosophical stance that unnecessary entropy — drift in definitions, tacit exceptions, ambiguous ownership, and decaying surfaces — is a manageable risk when made visible and reviewed. Justifies why explicit protocols must exist.
terms.boundaryNote: This is a conceptual governance layer. It does not assert perfect control, literal permanence, or technical entropy measurement.

terms.definition: The operational commitment to tie reviews to validity and dependency change rather than fashion cycles or arbitrary urgency. Expressed concretely as review cadence and entropy checks.
terms.boundaryNote: This term names review timing logic. It is not a mathematical algorithm, automated assessment, or scoring engine.

terms.definition: The explicit statement of what a protocol governs and what it does not govern. Out-of-scope items should point to the responsible instrument: another protocol, contract, legal process, or technical standard.
terms.boundaryNote: A scope boundary clarifies coverage. It does not assign legal responsibility or certify that a system is inside or outside compliance.

terms.definition: Any object used as evidence of compliance or as an operational interface to the protocol: documents, registers, URLs, schemas, dashboards, logs, or system screens. If it cannot be located, it is not yet an artifact.
terms.boundaryNote: An artifact supports reference traceability. Listing an artifact does not certify its quality, completeness, or compliance status.

terms.definition: A testable condition that distinguishes compliant operation from non-compliance. Criteria must be observable and attributable to an owner.
terms.boundaryNote: Acceptance criteria are internal governance conditions. They are not public compliance tests, readiness scores, or certification checks.

terms.definition: The scheduled and event-triggered timetable for revisiting a protocol's truth: whether it still matches reality, whether artifacts align, and whether exceptions remain justified.
terms.boundaryNote: Review cadence defines when review occurs. It does not guarantee outcomes, approve organizations, or open a submission workflow.

terms.definition: A structured examination during review for common drift modes: tacit exceptions, definition forks, surface drift, and ownership vacuums.
terms.boundaryNote: An entropy check is a review activity. It is not an automated scanner, compliance audit, or live readiness checklist.

terms.definition: The accumulation of undocumented divergence between authoritative protocol text, operational practice, and external-facing surfaces or data definitions.
terms.boundaryNote: Entropy drift identifies divergence between references and practice. It is not a scoring system, incident classification, or compliance finding.

terms.definition: The role responsible for keeping protocol text coherent, scheduling reviews, and maintaining the change log. Maintainers propose changes; they do not unilaterally alter obligations without approver action unless explicitly delegated.
terms.boundaryNote: Maintainer is a role within reference governance. It does not imply external authority, accreditation, or unilateral legal power.

terms.definition: The role authorized to approve material changes and time-bounded exceptions. Approvers bear accountability for scope and risk tradeoffs.
terms.boundaryNote: Approver is a role within a protocol governance process. It does not create public certification authority or third-party endorsement.

terms.definition: The role accountable for artifact integrity: availability, accuracy, and traceability to the protocol version they support.
terms.boundaryNote: Evidence steward is an internal accountability role. It does not provide external assurance, audit status, or compliance certification.

terms.definition: Any person or team obligated to operate under the protocol. Consumers are entitled to clarity, stable interfaces for change, and notice when obligations shift.
terms.boundaryNote: Consumer identifies a person or team operating under a protocol. It does not create a public registry or external participant status.

terms.definition: A documented, time-bounded deviation from a protocol requirement. Must state rationale, owner, expiry, and review trigger. Silent exceptions are defects, not informal flexibility.
terms.boundaryNote: Exception describes a documented deviation in protocol governance. It is not a waiver of legal obligations or external compliance approval.

terms.definition: A protocol update recorded with version number, date, author, summary, and accessible history. Semantic rules for major, minor, and patch are defined in the Methodology.
terms.boundaryNote: Versioned change supports citation and history. It does not create a dynamic API, public change registry, or submission system.

terms.definition: The degree to which operational reality matches the protocol's claims and artifacts. Validity is maintained by review, not by assertion.
terms.boundaryNote: Validity describes alignment between reference and reality. It is maintained by review and is not an external assurance opinion.

terms.definition: A site or document set intended to be cited, audited, and reused across contexts. This property imposes obligations: stable URLs, explicit updates, and definitional discipline.
terms.boundaryNote: Reference layer describes a citable document or site surface. It is not an MCP endpoint, dynamic API, or execution environment.

terms.definition: The structural readiness of an organization to demonstrate that its protocols, decisions, and knowledge assets were valid at the point of use. Strong evidence posture means an organization can answer: what was the governing reference, at what version, and who was responsible.
terms.boundaryNote: Evidence posture is a reference governance concept. It is not an audit opinion, assurance report, or proof of external compliance.

terms.definition: The practice of recording what changed in a reference system, when the change occurred, why it was made, and under whose authority — such that any prior state of the system can be identified and cited. The operational mechanism through which reference continuity is maintained.
terms.boundaryNote: Version discipline supports citation stability. It does not create a dynamic API, change registry, or external submission process.
